title: When the Visitor Turns
premise: Theo Joubert hosts a small-town overnight radio show, and one week after a listener's funeral, the dead start calling in — calm, grateful, wrong. When Theo plays back their own sleep recordings and hears a second voice answering questions Theo never asked aloud, they realize something crossed over during the station's ill-advised 'memorial broadcast' and has been learning to wear voices ever since. As the entity works through the town by impersonating its dead, Theo and an unlikely found family — a grieving widow, a disgraced deputy, and the station's insomniac engineer — uncover that the original invitation was made decades ago at the dry well behind the transmitter, and it can be closed before sunrise on the anniversary night. The ending costs Theo their voice and their show but gives the town back its honest grief: the dead stop calling, the well refills with silence, and Theo learns to speak again only in daylight.
about_author: Dominic Yarrow is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent six years answering calls from strangers who couldn't sleep. They write horror about voices, thresholds, and the people who stay on the line.

chapters.title: Dead Air, Live Callers
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. During the overnight shift, a caller named Marlene chats warmly — then Theo finds her obituary dated eight days ago. The emotional beat is quiet dread beneath professional composure; Theo keeps broadcasting because stopping feels like admitting the dark has a voice.

chapters.title: The Rules of the Booth
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo catalogs the phenomenon like a broadcaster: the calls come between 2 and 4 a.m., always polite, never asking for anything. Engineer Priya insists it's a prank; deputy-in-exile Ruth quietly confirms two more 'callers' are buried townsfolk. Beat: denial cracking into method.

chapters.title: What the Tape Caught
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Reviewing the night's logs, Priya finds forty minutes of studio silence where the waveform shows two voices — one of them answering questions in Theo's cadence. She plays it for Theo at dawn. Beat: the horror of hearing yourself used.

chapters.title: Marlene's Kitchen
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth visits Marlene's widower, Hal, who cheerfully reports his wife 'called last night to say she's fine.' The house smells of flowers kept too long. Beat: grief weaponized; Ruth recognizes the comfort as a trap because she once accepted it herself.

chapters.title: The Memorial Broadcast
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Flashback chapter: three weeks earlier, the station aired a live tribute reading names of the recently dead over the transmitter, mic open to callers. Theo remembers the moment the board lit up with no caller ID. Beat: guilt — they opened the door themselves.

chapters.title: Counting Doors
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo's compulsions surface: counting exits, keeping every light burning, sleeping with the recorder running. A call comes from Theo's own childhood home number, a mother's voice asking why Theo left. Beat: the entity stops being abstract and starts being intimate.

chapters.title: The Deputy Who Quit
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth's backstory: she resigned after ruling a drowning an accident she knew wasn't, and the drowned man called her every night afterward until she stopped answering. Now she sees the pattern repeating town-wide. Beat: shame transmuted into resolve; she joins Theo willingly.

chapters.title: Voices in Rotation
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Mapping the calls, Priya discovers each dead voice gets exactly one night, then goes silent forever — and the entity is working through the town's death list in order. Next week's name belongs to someone still alive. Beat: the rules have a direction, and time is short.

chapters.title: A Living Voice
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The entity calls using the voice of Danny Voss — alive, hospitalized, unresponsive since a fall near the old transmitter site. It asks Theo, gently, to read the memorial list again tonight. Beat: temptation framed as mercy; refusal as betrayal.

chapters.title: The Well Behind the Tower
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth and Theo hike to the capped well beside the transmitter mast and find offerings — coins, letters, a 1971 microphone cable — evidence of a generations-old practice of 'giving the well a voice.' Beat: the invitation wasn't an accident; it was a tradition gone rotten.

chapters.title: Hal's Confession
chapters.summary: Hal's POV (via recorded tape he leaves at the station). Hal admits that on the night of the memorial broadcast he asked the open line to let him hear Marlene one more time — a direct invitation, spoken into the tower's signal. Beat: the specific words that let it in, and the weight of ordinary longing.

chapters.title: Static Communion
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Priya isolates the second voice fully: it isn't any of the dead. It's older, patient, stitching together borrowed speech, and it has begun addressing Priya directly on tape, praising her careful ears. Beat: flattery as predation; Priya nearly answers.

chapters.title: The Town That Stopped Grieving
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interwoven. Half the town sleeps soundly now, comforted by nightly calls; the other half barricades their phones. A councilman proposes making the 'calls' official. Beat: complicity — a community choosing comfortable lies over hard truth, mirroring Ruth's old failure.

chapters.title: Danny Wakes Up Wrong
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Danny Voss regains consciousness speaking in a chorus of dead voices, asking staff to 'put him back on the air.' Ruth realizes the entity doesn't just imitate the dead — it can hold a living body at the threshold. Beat: stakes escalate from haunting to possession.

chapters.title: Anniversary Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Cross-referencing the 1971 cable and station archives, Theo finds the well was sealed fifty-three years ago on the coming Saturday — and the seal was a broadcast: a full night of silence transmitted into the ground. Beat: hope with a price; the counter-ritual requires a voice willing to go mute.

chapters.title: Rehearsal for Silence
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. The trio plans: at 2 a.m., transmit pure carrier-wave silence for the hours until sunrise while someone speaks the closing words at the well mouth. Whoever stands at the well will hear everything they've ever lost begging them to stop. Beat: dread braided with tenderness as they choose roles.

chapters.title: The Night Before
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Quiet chapter: the found family shares a last supper at the station, exchanging truths — Ruth's drowning, Priya's loneliness, Theo's runaway years. The phones stay off. Beat: love declared plainly, so the reader knows exactly what's at risk.

chapters.title: 2:00 A.M.
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The broadcast begins; the entity throws everything down the line — Marlene, Theo's mother, Ruth's drowned man, finally Danny's real voice screaming from the hospital. Priya holds the board; Ruth guards the road. Beat: siege horror, every defense tested.

chapters.title: At the Well Mouth
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. At the well, Theo hears the dead plead in voices they'd forgive anything for — then hears the entity drop all disguise and speak in its own sound, which no throat could make. Theo begins the closing words anyway. Beat: the climax of will against comfort.

chapters.title: Sunrise Refill
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. As dawn breaks, the well takes back what it lent: Danny wakes whole, the dead go quiet mid-sentence, and the transmitter feeds silence into the ground until the seal closes. But when Theo tries to speak the final word, nothing comes out. Beat: victory priced exactly as foretold.

chapters.title: Daylight Frequencies
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. Weeks later: the station pivots to daytime programming, Hal plants marigolds instead of waiting by the phone, and Ruth reopens the drowning case properly. Priya keeps one tape — the second voice — locked away, unanswered. Beat: healing without forgetting; vigilance as devotion.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo, voice half-returned and suited only for daylight, hosts a morning show where listeners call about ordinary troubles. On the last night of the year, Theo visits the well, says thank you in a whisper, and walks home before dark. Beat: peace earned, doors counted, lights left on for others.
